objective: Recognizing a measurement that falls outside the expected range
secondaryObjectives: Taking and recording temperature, pulse, respiration and blood pressure
Avoid a false oral temperature: wait if the resident has just had a hot or cold drink, chewed gum or smoked, and report a reading that does not fit how the resident looks
Choose a blood pressure cuff that fits: one that is too large reads falsely low and one that is too small reads falsely high, and the bladder should sit over the brachial artery
Observation versus interpretation, and why the aide reports the first
Reporting changes to the nurse: what, when and in what words
Recognizing an emergency and summoning help correctly
Recognizing abnormal changes in body functioning

brief.situation: 19:00 in a long-term care home. You are the nursing assistant doing evening vital signs on your hall. Mrs. Lindqvist in Room 14, 84, finished a cup of hot tea at 18:55. She says she felt 'woozy' when she stood up after supper.
handover: Care plan: atrial fibrillation (an irregular pulse) on apixaban, a blood thinner. Usual BP 130s/70s, pulse 70s and irregular. Small, thin arms: use the small adult cuff.
Report to the nurse at once: systolic BP under 100 or over 160, pulse under 60 or over 100, breathing over 24 a minute, temperature 37.8 C or higher, or any change in how she looks or acts.
She walks with a walker and toilets on her own. The nurse is on the hall doing the evening medication pass.
howItWorks: The clock runs in simulated time; study pace runs three simulated minutes per real minute. Pause any time.
Measuring takes a minute or two. Choose how you measure, decide what is out of range, and decide who needs to know and in what words.
Partway through you are asked to write what you found and what you did about it. A debrief scores what you did.

source.note: A slow upper GI bleed: untreated, she reaches shock about 1 h 50 min after 19:00, with a faint spell near 19:58. MSD gives the signs, not a rate. FLAG. Simplified teaching model written for exam practice; not a validated physiological model.
Above this she faints if she stands (about 19:08). MSD: syncope suggests significant hypovolemia. FLAG. Simplified teaching model written for exam practice; not a validated physiological model.
She becomes gray, sweaty and near-fainting and vomits coffee-ground material (about 19:58 untreated). FLAG. Simplified teaching model written for exam practice; not a validated physiological model.
Shock: unresponsive with a BP near 70 systolic. FLAG. Simplified teaching model written for exam practice; not a validated physiological model.
A manual BP with the cuff on: about 1.5 min.

cues.question: Which of your readings are outside her expected range, how sure are you that each was measured right, and what do you tell the nurse, when, and in what words?

parts.label: Out of range, and measured right
parts.criteria: Names the pulse over 100 (counted a full minute because it is irregular) and the BP falling toward or under 100 against her usual 130s as outside her range; knows a large cuff on a thin arm reads falsely low and a 30-second count of an irregular pulse can miss the fast rate; does not trust an oral temperature taken soon after hot tea.
parts.modelAnswer: Her pulse is over 100 and irregular, counted a full minute, and her BP is well below her usual 130s/70s, heading under 100: both outside her range, and with wooziness on standing. I used the small cuff because a large cuff on her thin arm reads falsely low, and I counted a full minute because her pulse is irregular. A temperature right after hot tea is not valid; I waited 15 minutes.

parts.label: What to say, and when
parts.criteria: Reports now, face to face, with observations (the numbers and how they were taken, what she said, the black sticky stool, pale and woozy) rather than a guess at a diagnosis; keeps her in bed and does not walk her; in an emergency calls for help without leaving her and lays her flat.
parts.modelAnswer: I tell the nurse now, in person: BP and pulse with how I took them, breathing, pale and woozy on standing, and she says her stool was black and sticky this afternoon. I don't tell her my guess; I give her what I saw and measured. Until the nurse comes I keep her in bed and use the commode, and if she starts to faint I lay her flat, raise her legs and use the call light and shout rather than leave her.

noProgress.rationale: A resident on a blood thinner with black stool and falling blood pressure still unseen by a nurse at the end of the case is bleeding unattended, so this case calls it harm.

expertPath.text: Look at her and ask how she feels: pale, woozy on standing, and black, sticky stool this afternoon.
BP with the small adult cuff and her irregular pulse counted a full minute: pulse over 100, BP well below her usual.
Find the nurse and give the findings, not a guess. Keep her in bed; bedside commode when she needs it.
Temperature now that 15 minutes have passed since her tea. The nurse assesses and calls the provider; objective note.

fell.headline: She fainted and fell
fell.body: A resident who is woozy on standing, with a fast pulse and a falling BP, stays in bed or uses a commode with you beside her. In an emergency, call for help from her side and lay her flat.

collapse.headline: She collapsed in bed
collapse.body: Out-of-range readings and black stool on a blood thinner were the cues. Find when the readings were taken, whether they were trusted, and when the nurse heard them.

sentEarly.headline: Measured, recognized, reported
sentEarly.body: Right cuff, a full-minute pulse, readings compared with her range, findings told to the nurse at once, and she stayed in bed. That is the expert path.

sentLate.headline: She got there, by a slower route
sentLate.body: Check how each reading was taken, how long the report took, whether it gave findings or a guess, and whether she walked while woozy.

time_up.headline: The nurse never saw her
time_up.body: An out-of-range reading is reported promptly. When the first answer is 'recheck later' and she keeps looking worse, report again with the numbers.

scoring.modelReasoning: Out of range means outside the facility's report parameters or clearly off the resident's own baseline. Her irregular pulse, counted a full 60 seconds, is over 100, and her BP measured with a cuff that fits her thin arm is falling from her usual 130s toward 100: report both now. A 30-second count of an irregular pulse and an oversized cuff both mislead, and an oral temperature soon after hot tea is not valid. The aide reports observations (numbers and how they were taken, what she said, the black sticky stool, pale and woozy), not a diagnosis, face to face and at once; keeps a woozy resident from walking; and in an emergency calls for help from the bedside and lays her flat rather than leaving her.

cuffQ.explain: An oversized cuff gives an artificially low reading and an undersized one an artificially high reading. Use the cuff that fits.
